sermon.title: Adding Love: God, Neighbors, and Enemies
sermon.series: Bible Morality Banned by Wimps and Born by Warriors
sermon.speaker: Pastor David G. Kincer
sermon.summary: The speaker says love must be added to faith: as a noun God is love (1 John 4:8), and as a verb we love God, neighbor, and enemies with action (Matthew 22; 5:44). Loving God means keeping commandments; loving neighbor means doing no harm (Romans 13:8). Luke 6’s turn-the-cheek pattern is for non-criminal neighbors who dislike you; sinners/criminals are a different subject requiring higher response as sons of the Father.
sermon.transcript_source: This transcript comes from YouTube’s automatic English captions, which supply the timing and the words. Punctuation, capitalization and paragraphing were added by hand, and obvious caption errors were corrected; his wording was not rewritten. “[unclear]” marks a word or name that was not clear. Caption fixes include “agape,” “Matthew 22:37” for “23:37” (he quotes love the Lord—misnamed chapter; kept his spoken flow in transcript where he said Matthew 23:37 but meaning is Deut/Matt 22:37—FLAG misnamed ref: he said “Matthew 23:37 love the Lord your God”), “1 John 5:3” for “1 John 53,” “acknowledge” for “ackowledge,” “sinners” for “siners,” “hillbilly” for “billion/heal bly.” Personal story of Detroit/Kentucky bullying and four court cases kept. Speaker not named—confirm Kincer.

chunks.text: Now, how to love God—the action, the verb. What do I do to love God? You see, do I just say I love God—that’s an action—or is there more to it? 1 John 5:3, this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. You see, I demonstrate my love for God by obeying his word, especially his laws. 2 John 6, this is love, that we walk after his commandments. chunks.section_question: How do you love your neighbor and yourself?
chunks.short_answer: He reads Romans 13:8—love does no harm to a neighbor, so love fulfills the law. If you obey God’s law and do nothing verbally, financially, or physically to hurt your neighbor, you fulfill loving God and neighbor. You must first not harm yourself.
chunks.text: You see, how is that done? Romans 13:8, love does no harm to a neighbor; therefore love fulfills the law. You see, if you love God you’ll obey his law. If you do nothing verbally, financially, physically to hurt your neighbor, you have fulfilled both loving God and your neighbor. Ain’t that beautiful? So love is an action. And before you’re going to be able to love your neighbor, you got to love yourself. You can’t do anything to verbally, physically, spiritually, financially harm yourself—then you can pass that on to others. Ain’t that beautiful? Hallelujah.

chunks.section_question: What personal example does he give of being cursed and insulted?
chunks.short_answer: He tells of moving from Kentucky to Detroit, mocked as a dumb hillbilly with an accent, excluded from baseball, falsely accused in court four times—and applies Luke 6: turn the other cheek, and if they take your cloak do not withhold the tunic, digging into what that means.
chunks.text: When I went to Detroit from Kentucky, those northerners hated me. They laughed at me and mocked at me. I had an accent and I was a dumb hillbilly, and they called me a dumb hillbilly. And I had never experienced the world yet. I was down there in that cozy little country setting, and man, no bullies, no gangs, no nothing. And to be a hillbilly—never amount to nothing. You—I didn’t even know how to play baseball. Never played baseball in my life. And so they tag you, you know—you’re this, you’re that—and they despise you. They don’t want you on their baseball team. You ain’t know how to hold a bat, you stupid hillbilly. Pray for those who spitefully use you or insult you, slander you, falsely accuse you. I’ve been to court four times from people falsely accusing me, slandering me, defaming my character—four times. To him who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other. You know, somebody hate you so much because you’re a hillbilly so long that you finally go, I’m not a stupid hillbilly, and they smack you upside the head—you are too. Come to your senses. Supposed to turn the other cheek. He who takes your cloak, do not withhold your tunic. Cloak is a coat like we wear, and the tunic is an inner garment. You know, so basically they take your coat and you give them your tunic—you’re naked. And the Bible’s against running around naked, and most people in society don’t want you run around naked, because most of us aren’t worth looking at naked. You know, people read this and you got to understand—you got to dig into this to know what he’s talking about.

chunks.section_question: Who is the Luke 6 illustration for—neighbors or criminals?
chunks.short_answer: He says it is for brother and neighbor who are not criminals—they may dislike your race, hair, talk, or hometown (his Appalachian hillbilly example) but are not stealing or beating you. Loving to get love back is what sinners do.
chunks.text: You see, so obviously this is an illustration of how to love your brother and your neighbor who is not criminals. They just don’t like you. Maybe they don’t like your race. Maybe they don’t like the color of your hair. Maybe they don’t like the way you talk, where you’re from—like this stupid hillbilly from the Appalachian mountains. But they’re not out stealing from you. They’re not out beating you up, kicking you on the ground. They’re not criminals. He goes on to say this: if you love—he’s starting another subject—to receive. If you give out things to get back, you love to get love, you lend to get something out of the act of lending, if you do good because you want that person to acknowledge you and do something for you—he says, what do you more than others? Sinners do that. Now he switches to sinners.

chunks.section_question: What does he mean by sinners/criminals as a switched subject?
chunks.short_answer: He says sinners are malicious, purposeful violators of God’s word—another word is criminal. Sons of the Father do better than sinners: no verbal attack back, try to avoid beating back. He says most of the American church is not close to that maturity and must get uncomfortable to change the nation.
